{{Short description|Language of Baekje}} {{Infobox language | name = Baekje | altname = Paekche | states = [[Paekche]] | region = [[Korea]] | era = 4th–7th centuries | familycolor = altaic | fam1 = [[Koreanic languages|Koreanic]] | lc1 = pkc | ld1 = Paekche | lc2 = xpp | ld2 = Puyo-Paekche | glotto = paek1234 | glottorefname = Paekche | map = Three Kingdoms of Korea Map.png | mapcaption = The Three Kingdoms of Korea, with Baekje in green. }} The language of the kingdom of [[Baekje]] (4th–7th centuries), one of the [[Three Kingdoms of Korea]], is poorly attested, and scholars differ on whether one or two languages were used. However, at least some of the material appears to be a variety of Old Korean.{{sfnp|Vovin|2010|pp=240}} == Description in early texts == Baekje was preceded in southwestern Korea by the [[Mahan confederacy]]. The Chinese ''[[Records of the Three Kingdoms]]'' (3rd century) states that the [[Mahan language]] differed from that of [[Goguryeo]] to the north and the other [[Samhan]] ('Three Han') to the east, [[Byeonhan confederacy|Byeonhan]] and [[Jinhan confederacy|Jinhan]], whose languages were said to resemble each other. However, the ''[[Book of the Later Han]]'' (5th century) speaks of differences between the languages of Byeonhan and Jinhan.{{sfnp|Lee|Ramsey|2011|pp=35–36}} Historians believe that Baekje was established by immigrants from [[Goguryeo]] who took over Mahan, while Byeonhan and Jinhan were succeeded by [[Gaya confederacy|Gaya]] and [[Silla]] respectively. According to ''[[Book of Liang]]'' (635), the language of Baekje was similar to that of Goguryeo.{{sfnp|Lee|Ramsey|2011|p=44}} Chapter 49 of the ''[[Book of Zhou]]'' (636) says of Baekje:{{sfnp|Vovin|2005|p=119}} {{blockquote|text={{lang|lzh|王姓夫餘氏，號於羅瑕，民呼為鞬吉支，夏言竝王也。}}
The king belongs to the Puyŏ clan; the gentry call him {{lang|und-Hani|於羅瑕}}; commoners call him {{lang|und-Hani|鞬吉支}}. In Chinese it means 'king'.}} Based in this passage and some Baekje words cited in the Japanese history {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Shoki]]}} (720), many scholars, beginning with Kōno Rokurō and later [[Kim Bang-han]], have argued that the kingdom of Baekje was bilingual, with the gentry speaking a [[Puyŏ languages|Puyŏ language]] and the common people a [[Han languages|Han language]].{{sfnp|Kōno|1987|pp=84–85}}{{sfnp|Kim|2009|p=766}}{{sfnp|Beckwith|2004|pp=20–21}} The [[Linguist List]] defined two codes for these languages, and these have been taken over into the [[ISO 639-3]] registry.{{sfnp|Linguist List|2010}} == Linguistic data == There are no extant texts in the Baekje language.{{sfnp|Nam|2012|p=49}} The primary contemporary lexical evidence comes from a few glosses in Chinese and Japanese histories, as well as proposed etymologies for old place names.{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|p=223}} === ''Nihon Shoki'' === The Japanese history {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Shoki]]}}, compiled in the early 8th century from earlier documents, including some from Baekje, records 42 Baekje words. These are transcribed as [[Old Japanese]] syllables, which are restricted to the form (C)V, limiting the precision of the transcription.{{sfnp|Bentley|2000|pp=419–420}} {| class="wikitable" |+ Family and society words from the ''Nihon Shoki''{{sfnp|Bentley|2000|pp=424–427, 436–438}} |- ! rowspan="2" | Gloss ! rowspan="2" | Transcription ! colspan="3" | Comparison |- ! imported many artifacts from Baekje and the [[Gaya confederacy]], and several of the above matching Old Japanese forms are believed to have been borrowed from Baekje at that time.{{sfnp|Bentley|2001|p=59}} Such borrowing would also explain the fact that words such as {{transliteration|ojp|kaso2}} 'father', {{transliteration|ojp|ki2}} 'fortress', {{transliteration|ojp|ko2po2ri}} 'district' and {{transliteration|ojp|kuti}} 'hawk' are limited to Western Old Japanese, with no cognates in [[Eastern Old Japanese]] or [[Ryukyuan languages]].{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|pp=226–227}} Moreover, for some words, like 'father' and 'mother', there are alternative words in Old Japanese that are attested across the [[Japonic languages|Japonic family]] ({{transliteration|ojp|titi}} and {{transliteration|ojp|papa}} respectively).{{sfnp|Vovin|2010|pp=92–94}} Bentley lists these words, as well as {{transliteration|ojp|kuma}} 'bear' and {{transliteration|ojp|suki2}} 'village', as loans into Old Japanese from Baekje.{{sfnp|Bentley|2001|pp=59–60}} [[Alexander Vovin]] argues that the only Baekje words from the ''Nihon Shoki'' found throughout Japonic, such as {{transliteration|pkc|sema}} 'island' and {{transliteration|pkc|kuma}} 'bear', are those also common to Koreanic.{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|pp=226–227}} === Other histories === The Middle Korean text {{transliteration|okm|[[Yongbieocheonga]]}} transcribes the name of the old Baekje capital 'Bear Ford' as {{transliteration|pkc|kwomá nolo}}, closely matching two of the words from the {{transliteration|ojp|Nihon Shoki}}.{{sfnp|Lee|Ramsey|2011|p=45}} Chapter 49 of the Chinese ''[[Book of Zhou]]'' (636) cites three Baekje words:{{sfnp|Vovin|2005|p=119}}{{efn|Names represented phonetically with Chinese characters are transcribed using [[Baxter's transcription for Middle Chinese|William H. Baxter's transcription for Middle Chinese]].}} * {{transliteration|ltc|ʔyo-la-hae}} ({{lang|und-Hani|於羅瑕}}) 'king' (used by the gentry) * {{transliteration|tlc|kjon-kjit-tsye}} ({{lang|und-Hani|鞬吉支}}) 'king' (used by commoners) * {{transliteration|ltc|ʔyo-ljuwk}} ({{lang|und-Hani|於陸}}) 'queen' These may be the same words as {{transliteration|pkc|orikoke}} 'king', {{transliteration|pkc|ki1si}} 'ruler' and {{transliteration|pkc|oruku}} 'queen' respectively, found in the {{transliteration|ja|Nihon Shoki}}.{{sfnp|Vovin|2005|pp=121–124}} Chapter 54 of the ''[[Book of Liang]]'' (635) gives four Baekje words:{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|pp=232–233}} * {{transliteration|ltc|kuH-mae}} ({{lang|und-Hani|固麻}}) 'ruling fortress' * {{transliteration|ltc|yem-luX}} ({{lang|und-Hani|檐魯}}) 'settlement' * {{transliteration|ltc|pjuwk-syaem}} ({{lang|und-Hani|複衫}}) 'short jacket' * {{transliteration|ltc|kwon}} ({{lang|und-Hani|褌}}) 'pants' None of these have Koreanic etymologies, but Vovin suggests that the first might be cognate with Old Japanese {{transliteration|ojp|ko2me2}} 'enclose', and the second with Old Japanese {{transliteration|ojp|ya}} 'house' + {{transliteration|ojp|maro2}} 'circle'.{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|pp=232–233}}{{sfnp|Vovin|2017|p=13}} He views this as limited evidence for Kōno's two-language hypothesis, and suggests that the language of the commoners may have been the same [[Peninsular Japonic]] language reflected by [[placename glosses in the Samguk sagi|placename glosses in the ''Samguk sagi'']] from the northern part of Baekje captured by Goguryeo in the 5th century.{{sfnp|Vovin|2013|pp=224, 233}}{{sfnp|Vovin|2017|p=12}} The Baekje placenames in chapter 37 of the {{transliteration|ko|[[Samguk sagi]]}} are not glossed, but several of them include the form {{lang|und-Hani|夫里}} {{transliteration|ltc|pju-liX}}, which has been compared with later Korean {{transliteration|ko|pul}} 'plain'.{{sfnp|Lee|Ramsey|2011|pp=44–45}} === Wooden tablets === Wooden tablets dated to the late Baekje era have been discovered by archaeologists, and some of them involve the rearrangement of [[Classical Chinese]] words according to native syntax. From this data, the word order of Baekje appears to have been similar to that of Old Korean. Unlike in Silla texts, however, no uncontroversial evidence of non-Chinese grammatical morphemes has been found.{{sfnp|Lee|2017|pp=290–298}} Compared to Silla tablets, Baekje tablets are far more likely to employ conventional Classical Chinese syntax and vocabulary without any native influence.{{sfnp|Lee|2017|pp=299–301}} The tablets also give the names of 12 locations and 77 individuals.{{sfnp|Lee|2017|p=276}} A total of 147 phonographic characters have been identified from these proper nouns, but this is insufficient to allow a reconstruction of the phonology.{{sfnp|Lee|2017|p=362}} Lee Seungjae suggests that a tablet found in the Baekje-built temple of [[Mireuksa]], originally thought to be a list of personal names, appears to record native numerals, possibly a series of dates, using phonograms (both phonetically and semantically adapted). Although the tablet is dated to the early [[Later Silla]] period, postdating the 660 fall of Baekje, its orthography differs from conventional [[Old Korean#Orthography|Old Korean orthography]]. In the extant Silla texts, a native numeral is written by a logogram-phonogram sequence. The numerals appear Koreanic, with a suffix [[File:Old Korean 邑 variant.jpg|20px]] {{IPA|*-(ə)p}} that may be cognate to the Early Middle Korean ordinal suffix {{IPA|*-m}}.{{sfnp|Lee|2017|pp=87–99}}{{efn|The character 𢀳 ([[File:Old Korean 邑 variant.svg|20px]]) is visually similar to and likely based on {{lang|und-Hani|邑}}.}} {| class="wikitable" |+Potential Baekje numerals{{sfnp|Lee|2017|pp=89, 96}} |- !
